text:
In the autumn of the university’s sesquicentennial, a forensic architect drilled a core sample out of the brutalist ziggurat known as Moppett Hall and discovered that the original contractors, in the strike-plagued summer of 1974, had omitted the waterproofing membrane entirely. On the blueprints, the membrane was a confident cerulean line. In reality, there was only petrified mastic, vintage Schlitz pull-tabs, and forty-eight years of capillary action.

For the Department of Comparative Literature, occupying the upper tiers, the revelation offered perverse vindication. For decades, facilities managers had insisted that the clamminess of their offices—the curling paperbacks, the mushroomy breath from the grates—was either psychological projection or the result of storing too many nineteenth-century German monographs in one quadrant.

“We have been vindicated,” Miriam Vance, the department chair, announced at the October faculty meeting. A scholar of Franco-Flemish manuscripts with a wan, archival complexion, she held up the report. “We are not crazy. We are simply unsealed.”

Arthur Lowe, whose specialty was the late-Romantic fragment and whose office sat beneath the northeast scupper, raised a hand. “Does the report specify a timeline, Miriam? The plaster behind my filing cabinet resembles a relief map of the Pyrenees.”

“Capital Projects is mobilizing,” Miriam said with grim, borrowed authority. “They call it an Envelope Intervention. They anticipate minimal disruption to the pedagogical mission.”

The mobilization began the following Tuesday at seven in the morning, with a sound like a giant dentist drilling into the molar of the earth.

Arthur was grading midterms on Baudelaire when the first diamond-tipped rotary saw bit into the concrete exterior three feet from his head. The vibration ascended his shins and set his teeth chattering at a frequency that made drinking his Darjeeling impossible. Outside his window, a mast climber groaned up the façade, bearing two men in neon vests and respirators who regarded Arthur’s book-lined sanctuary with the flat gaze of deep-sea divers examining a sunken galleon. Within an hour, they had stapled opaque polyethylene over his window, plunging the room into a permanent, milky twilight that smelled of hot vinyl.

By Thanksgiving, Moppett Hall was entirely swaddled in this shroud, lashed to scaffolding that sang whenever the wind came off the river. Entering required navigating a plywood tunnel that acted as a sluice when it rained, funneling runoff into the lobby where yellow blowers roared day and night.

Under the acoustic and atmospheric pressure, faculty tensions calcified. In the mailroom—relocated to a former janitor’s closet—disputes broke out over the six portable dehumidifiers.

Julian Cross, an assistant professor of environmental humanities, became the department’s Cassandra. He arrived each morning wearing a valved N95 mask and carrying a handheld particulate counter.

“Twelve hundred parts per million of volatile organic compounds outside Room 304,” Julian announced in early December, cornering Arthur. His eyes were bright with terror and theoretical vindication. “They’re injecting hydrophobic polyurethane grout into the expansion joints. Isocyanates cross-link with proteins in human lung tissue, Arthur. We are literally being laminated from the inside out.”

“I’m sure Physical Plant vetted the safety sheets,” Arthur said, though he had woken with a metallic taste in his mouth.

“Physical Plant is an apparatus of institutional necropolitics,” Julian muffled through his respirator. “Look at Helena’s philodendron.”

Outside the office of Helena Rostova, the senior Slavicist, a potted *Monstera* sat in the hall, its leaves speckled with gray dust and drooping like the ears of a beaten hound. Helena emerged, wrapped in an Orenburg shawl, clutching black tea.

“In Brno, during the normalization,” she said in her gravelly contralto, “they replaced the steam pipes beneath the philosophical faculty while classes were in session. For two winters, we taught Pushkin in overcoats, sitting on planks over an open trench. You Americans expect a building to be a womb. A building is just a truce with the weather.”

“A truce implies bilateral compliance, Helena,” Julian said. “My sinuses are bleeding.”

“Eat more beets,” Helena advised, shuffling back into her synthetic twilight.

Even Helena’s stoicism was tested in January, when the intervention entered “Phase Two: Substrate Stabilization and Liquid Membrane Application.”

To apply the membrane—a tarry compound smelling of burning tires—contractors stripped away the exterior panels, leaving offices separated from winter by metal studs and damp fiberglass. The thermostats went mad. Arthur’s office plunged to fifty-two degrees, while Miriam’s became an eighty-six-degree conservatory where medieval facsimiles cracked like pistol shots.

Worse was the liquid membrane itself, which proved an ambitious migrant. Seeking the path of least resistance through the honeycombed concrete, the viscous fluid seeped inward.

It appeared first as a dark blister above the chalkboard during Arthur’s colloquium on the Aesthetics of Ruin. A student was reading a paper on Diderot when the blister swelled to the size of a grapefruit, trembled in sympathy with a jackhammer upstairs, and burst with a soft, obscene *plop*. A ribbon of glossy black tar oozed down the slate, bisecting a diagram of the hermeneutic circle. The smell of refined bitumen filled the room.

“Perhaps,” Arthur said, his throat raw, “we might adjourn to the divinity school coffee shop.”

By February, the department had fractured into a diaspora. Office hours were held in the science library basement or pacing the muddy quad in Gore-Tex. Miriam began wearing a white hard hat in the hallways. Julian submitted a twelve-page workers’ compensation claim detailing “epistemic and bronchial trauma,” accompanied by macro photographs of a mold colony shaped like the Peloponnese behind his bookcase.

Even Arthur found his scholarship buckling. Finishing a monograph on the July Monarchy, he caught himself using words like *spalling*, *efflorescence*, and *delamination* to describe Sainte-Beuve’s prose. He dreamed his own skin lacked a vapor barrier, that campus slush was seeping through his pores, turning his bones to wet chalk.

The crisis reached its apogee in March during a torrential thaw. Rain fell on two feet of snow, and the contractors—waiting on back-ordered copper flashing—had relied on blue tarpaulins weighted with concrete blocks to protect the fourth floor.

At eleven in the morning, the wind caught the primary tarpaulin like a spinnaker and peeled it back with a sound like a cannon shot.

Arthur, Miriam, Julian, and Helena were in the windowless lounge, huddled around a space heater, reviewing graduate admissions files. First came a hollow roar in the ceiling plenum. Then came the water. It arrived through the acoustic tiles in braided, dirty-brown columns, smelling of wet pigeon feathers and forty-eight-year-old dust. One column struck the table, saturating thirty-two applicant dossiers. Another hit the space heater with a violent hiss, plunging the room into acrid steam before the breaker tripped and the lights died.

Illuminated only by the exit sign, the four scholars sat frozen. Water cascaded off Miriam’s hard hat like runoff from a gargoyle. A soggy GRE report floated into Julian’s lap.

“Well,” Miriam said calmly into the darkness, stripped at last of administrative optimism. “That will certainly simplify the shortlist.”

An hour later, the Dean arrived with Kyle, the Associate Vice President for Capital Projects, whose Patagonia vest was dry and whose expression was a masterclass in liability management. Behind them, men with wet-dry vacuums slurped at the carpet.

“What we’re looking at here,” Kyle explained, gesturing with a laser pointer, “is an unforeseen meteorological synergy. The good news is that the Phase Three interior guttering system is engineered for a hundred-year hydrostatic load.”

“When,” Arthur asked, his damp tweed steaming, “is Phase Three?”

Kyle consulted a rubber-encased iPad. “Supply chain issues with the mullions have pushed re-glazing to late Q3. So, substantial completion by October. Meanwhile, we’ll bring in negative-air scrubbers and encapsulate the fourth-floor drywall.”

“Encapsulate,” Julian repeated hollowly. “You’re going to seal the moisture inside the walls.”

“We’re going to manage the micro-climate,” Kyle corrected gently. “And the Dean’s office has authorized a five-hundred-dollar stipend per faculty member for noise-canceling headphones.”

A heavy quiet settled over the faculty. Arthur looked at his colleagues. They smelled of wet wool and fungicide. They had spent their lives studying texts that survived the burning of Alexandria and the bombings of Dresden; they were custodians of remnants that endured despite the incompetence of history. To demand a dry office now seemed almost vulgar—a failure of genre.

“Does the stipend cover Sony,” Julian asked quietly, “or are we restricted to the preferred vendor list for Bose?”

“Any retailer,” the Dean said quickly. “Just save the receipt.”

Spring came in April, registered inside Moppett Hall only by the polyethylene glowing a warmer yellow, and the contractors’ radio changing from classic rock to Dominican bachata.

On a Tuesday in May, Arthur sat in his office wearing his Sony headphones—reducing the tuck-pointers to a distant hum—reading proofs. A knock vibrated through the doorframe.

Miriam stood on the threshold holding two paper cups, a golf umbrella hooked over her wrist like a bishop’s crosier. “I brought you a cortado,” she said, stepping over a dehumidifier hose. “And the new schedule.”

Arthur took the cup. The plaster behind his desk had been cut away to let the studs “breathe,” revealing rusted plumbing stacks. He had grown fond of the view, propping an engraving of Piranesi’s *Carceri* against a galvanized pipe.

“Are we being un-bagged for Commencement?” Arthur asked.

“September,” Miriam said, sitting down. “Apparently, the November primer was incompatible with the March sealant. It’s blistering on the south elevation. They have to sandblast it off and start again with a silane-siloxane penetrant.”

Outside the milky plastic, the shadow of a workman passed, whistling along to the bachata, followed by the rhythmic *slap-slap* of a trowel.

“Silane-siloxane,” Arthur murmured, testing the trochaic weight of the compound. “Do we think that will hold?”

Miriam looked up at the ceiling, where a fresh, amber water stain shaped like the Duchy of Burgundy was drying around the sprinkler head.

“Kyle says it carries a twenty-year warranty,” she said. “Which means it should last just long enough for both of us to retire, Arthur, and become emeritus ghosts in the library basement.”

She raised her paper cup; he touched his to hers. Above them, a hammer drill began to chatter against the lintels, a steady pulse that shook a fine snow of gypsum dust onto Arthur’s desk calendar, burying the rest of the semester in white.
